lessons.unit: S1-S6: Statistics
lessons.title: Populations, samples and sampling methods
lessons.bigQuestion: Can a small group tell us the truth about a whole population?
objectives: Distinguish a population from a sample
Describe random, systematic and stratified sampling
Use a sample to estimate a population, including capture-recapture
successCriteria: All: explain why a sample can be biased and how to reduce bias
Most: choose and carry out stratified sampling
Some: estimate a population from a sample, including capture-recapture
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography and biology: fieldwork sampling
lessons.smsc: Justice ('adl) and fairness: a fair survey represents everyone, not just the people it is easy to ask.

keywords.def: the whole group being studied
a smaller group selected from the population
an unfair preference that makes a sample unrepresentative

teach.heading: Sampling vocabulary
bullets: Population: everyone or everything we want to know about
Sample: the part we actually measure
Random: every member has an equal chance
Bias: some members are more likely to be chosen
teach.note: Ask for a population in the pupils' world (all pupils in the school) and a poor sample (only the football team). Connect to the idea of fairness in the smsc line.

teach.heading: Sampling methods

head: Method
How it works
Strength
Weakness
rows: Every member has an equal chance (numbers from a list or hat)
Choose every kth member after a random start
Sample each group in proportion to its size

teach.note: Pupils copy the table and then explain which method they would use for a survey on school meals. Higher: stratified sampling must be carried out with proportional calculation.

teach.heading: Stratified sample

model.problem: A school has 600 pupils: Year 7 140, Year 8 120, Year 9 130, Year 10 110, Year 11 100. A stratified sample of 60 is needed. How many from each year?

teach.note: The numbers divide neatly here; in general round and check the total. Within each year, choose the pupils at random.

teach.heading: Capture-recapture

model.problem: A biologist catches 60 fish in a lake, marks them and releases them. Later she catches 50 fish and 8 are marked. Estimate the population of the lake.
steps: Fraction marked in the second sample = 8/50
Assume this equals the fraction in the whole lake: 60 ÷ N

teach.note: Higher only. Assumptions: the marked fish have mixed with the others, no fish enter, leave, die or lose marks. The formula is N = (marked first × second sample) ÷ marked in second.

teach.heading: Hinge: bias

check.q: Which sample is most likely to be biased when finding the healthiest foods people eat?
options: 100 people chosen randomly from the electoral register
100 people leaving a health food shop
100 people chosen at random from several towns
A stratified sample by age and area
check.why: People leaving a health food shop are more likely to eat healthily, so the sample is not representative.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask how to improve it (random sample from the whole population). ANSWERS: practice: 14, 12, 13, 11, 10; 40 × 60 ÷ 5 = 480; 24/80 × 600 = 180; biased by time and place, and only commuters. exit: bigger samples reduce chance variation; it often over-represents some people. core: take every 20th name after a random start between 1 and 20; stratified gives every year its fair share; N = 50 × 40 ÷ 4 = 500, assuming the marked fish mixed fully and the population did not change; extend: self-selected, small, possibly biased by incentive. homework: pupils' design.

practice: A school has 600 pupils (Y7 140, Y8 120, Y9 130, Y10 110, Y11 100). Find a stratified sample of 60.
40 fish are marked and released. A sample of 60 contains 5 marked. Estimate the population.
A random sample of 80 pupils finds that 24 walk to school. Estimate the number of walkers among 600 pupils.
A survey is carried out only at 8 am outside a train station. Give two reasons for bias.
independent: Core: a) Explain how to select a systematic sample of 30 from 600 pupils on a list. b) Compare stratified and simple random sampling for the survey of 600 pupils.
Extend: A lake survey: 50 marked and released; second sample of 40 contains 4 marked. Estimate the number, and say what assumption you made. Why might the estimate be too high or too low?
Stretch: A company claims that '90% of customers are happy' after surveying 20 people who left reviews. Give three criticisms.
exit: Why is a sample of 1000 better than a sample of 10?
State one disadvantage of convenience sampling.
Big question: Can a small group tell us the truth about a whole population?
lessons.homework: Design a fair survey to find out how Year 10 pupils get to school. State the population, the method and the sample size.
lessons.send: SEND: give the sampling fraction as a fraction line and a table to fill; use physical names in a hat. EAL: 'population', 'sample', 'bias'. Stretch: criticise real-world survey claims. Higher-only: stratified sampling calculations and capture-recapture.
lessons.board: Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9-1) Mathematics (1MA1), Higher tier

lessons.unit: S1-S6: Statistics
lessons.title: Tables, charts and time series
lessons.bigQuestion: Which chart tells the truest story?
objectives: Draw and interpret pie charts and stem-and-leaf diagrams
Interpret bar charts and time series, including trend and seasonality
Spot misleading graphs
successCriteria: All: calculate pie chart angles and read a stem-and-leaf diagram
Most: describe the trend and seasonal pattern of a time series
Some: identify misleading scales and give a fair conclusion
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography and PSHE: reading data in the news
lessons.smsc: Honesty (sidq): presenting data so that it is not misleading.

keywords.def: a circle divided into sectors in proportion to frequencies
data recorded at regular times
the general direction of the data over time

teach.heading: Pie chart

model.problem: 120 pupils travel to school: 45 walk, 30 take the bus, 25 come by car, 20 cycle. Find the pie chart angles.

teach.note: Show the 'angle per person' step. Read: a sector of 90° is a quarter of the pupils, so 30.

teach.heading: Stem-and-leaf

model.problem: Draw an ordered stem-and-leaf diagram for 23, 25, 31, 34, 34, 38, 42, 45, 47, 51, 53, 58. Find the median and range.
steps: 12 values: median is between the 6th (38) and 7th (42): 40

teach.note: The key is essential. The diagram shows the shape of the data and keeps every value. Back-to-back diagrams compare two sets.

teach.heading: A time series: kilograms of dates sold
teach.note: Describe two features: an upward trend (each year higher than the last) and a seasonal pattern (Q4 is the highest each year, Q2 the lowest). Predict: Year 4 Q4 might be about 270, but this is an extrapolation and uncertain.

teach.heading: Hinge: pie chart

check.q: 300 people: 75 chose tea. The pie chart angle for tea is:
check.why: 75 ÷ 300 = 1/4, and 1/4 of 360° = 90°. 75° uses the frequency as the angle; 25° is the percentage.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask for the angle per person (1.2°).

teach.heading: Misleading scales

misconception.wrong: A bar chart showing sales of 50 and 55 looks as if sales have doubled.
misconception.right: Check the vertical axis: starting at 48 not 0 exaggerates a 10% rise.

teach.note: Show the same chart with a zero baseline. Ask pupils to find three ways a graph can mislead: truncated axis, uneven scale, 3D effects. ANSWERS: practice: 135°, 90°, 75°, 60°; median 40; upward trend with a Q4 peak each year; 90°. exit: 80°; trend or seasonality. core: French 144°, Spanish 120°, Arabic 96°; medians compared with a conclusion. extend: check the axis starts at zero, scales are even and the time period is representative. stretch: trend is the general direction; seasonality is a repeating pattern linked to the season. homework: pupil work.

practice: 120 pupils: walk 45, bus 30, car 25, cycle 20. Find the pie chart angles.
Draw a stem-and-leaf for 23, 25, 31, 34, 34, 38, 42, 45, 47, 51, 53, 58 and find the median.
Use the dates table to describe the trend and the seasonal pattern.
300 people: 75 chose tea. Find the angle for tea.
independent: Core: a) 90 pupils choose a language: French 36, Spanish 30, Arabic 24. Pie chart angles. b) Draw a back-to-back stem-and-leaf for two sets (give your own two lists of 8 numbers) and compare medians.
Extend: A newspaper graph shows crime falling steeply. Describe what to check on the graph.
Stretch: The time series of monthly rainfall for a town: describe what trend and seasonality mean and what may cause them.
exit: Find the pie chart angle for 20 pupils out of 90.
Write down a feature of a time series.
Big question: Which chart tells the truest story?
lessons.homework: Find a chart from a newspaper or website and comment in four sentences on whether it is fair or misleading.
lessons.send: SEND: give angle per item as a fraction line and protractor guides. EAL: 'trend', 'seasonal', 'key'. Stretch: draw a frequency polygon from grouped data.
lessons.board: Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9-1) Mathematics (1MA1), Higher tier

lessons.unit: S1-S6: Statistics
lessons.title: Histograms with unequal class widths
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do we plot frequency density instead of frequency?
objectives: Calculate frequency density
Draw a histogram with unequal class widths
Read frequencies and estimate values from a histogram
successCriteria: All: calculate frequency density and frequency
Most: draw and read a histogram with unequal classes
Some: estimate a median or a number in a range from a histogram
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography and Biology: grouped data such as heights
lessons.smsc: Fair comparison: area must stand for amount, not height alone.

keywords.def: frequency ÷ class width
the size of a class interval
a chart where the area of each bar represents the frequency

starter: Find the class width of 10 < t ≤ 30.

teach.heading: From a table to a histogram
teach.note: Higher only. Frequency density = frequency ÷ class width. The area of each bar equals the frequency. The 160 < h ≤ 180 bar is wide so its height is lower than 30.

teach.heading: Reading a histogram

model.problem: A histogram has bars: 0-10 with density 1.6, 10-30 with density 2.4, 30-40 with density 3.0 and 40-60 with density 0.9. Find each frequency, the total and the median.
steps: Median is the 56th value: cumulative 16 then 64, so it lies in 10-30

teach.note: Interpolation assumes the data are spread evenly in the class. The number in the 20-35 range would be 10 × 2.4 + 5 × 3.0 = 39.

teach.heading: Hinge: frequency

check.q: A bar has width 5 and frequency density 4. The frequency is:
check.why: Frequency = frequency density × class width = 20. 9 adds them; 0.8 divides.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask which bar would be wider if the frequency were the same but the class twice as wide.

teach.heading: Estimating a number

model.problem: Using the heights table, estimate how many people have height between 165 cm and 180 cm.
steps: 165-180 is part of the class 160-180 with density 1.5

teach.note: Assumes even spread within the class. Compare with fractions of the class: 15/20 of 30 = 22.5.

teach.heading: Height equals frequency

misconception.wrong: The 160-180 bar is tallest since it has the most people, 30.
misconception.right: Height shows frequency density: 1.5, lower than the 150-160 bar (2.0), because the class is wider.

teach.note: Always ask 'what is on the vertical axis?' and use area. ANSWERS: practice: 0.8, 2.0, 1.5, 0.3; frequencies 16, 48, 30, 18; 22.5; area must represent frequency since classes differ in width. exit: 0.9; the class width changes so the height measures density. core: densities 1.5, 3.6, 1.5, 0.3; between 25 and 40: 15 × 1.5 = 22.5; modal class 10-20 (highest density). extend: total 93, median is the 46.5th: 15 + 36 = 51 at 20 so it lies in 10-20: 10 + (46.5 - 15) ÷ 36 × 10 = 18.75. stretch: 18 and 18, so the remaining total is 56 - 36 = 20. homework: histogram drawn.

practice: Complete the density column: 8, 20, 30, 6 for classes of width 10, 10, 20, 20.
From density 1.6, 2.4, 3.0 and 0.9 with widths 10, 20, 10, 20 find the frequencies.
Estimate the number in 165-180 cm.
State why a histogram needs frequency density.
independent: Core: a) Quiz times: 0 < t ≤ 10: 15; 10 < t ≤ 20: 36; 20 < t ≤ 40: 30; 40 < t ≤ 80: 12. Find the frequency densities and the number between 25 and 40 minutes. b) State the modal class.
Extend: Estimate the median time for the quiz.
Stretch: A histogram has the bar 20-30 with height 1.8 and 30-50 with height 0.9 and total frequency 56. Find the frequencies in these bars and the remaining total.
exit: Find the frequency density of a class 40 < t ≤ 60 with frequency 18.
Explain why bar height is not the frequency when the classes are unequal.
Big question: Why do we plot frequency density instead of frequency?
lessons.homework: Draw a histogram of the quiz times data on graph paper with a labelled density axis.
lessons.send: SEND: use a calculation table with columns for width, frequency and density; use squared paper. EAL: 'density', 'width', 'frequency'. Stretch: reconstruct the table from a drawn histogram with a given scale. Higher-only: this whole lesson (S3).
lessons.board: Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9-1) Mathematics (1MA1), Higher tier

lessons.unit: S1-S6: Statistics
lessons.title: Cumulative frequency, quartiles and box plots
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a single graph show the middle and the spread of a large data set?
objectives: Draw a cumulative frequency graph
Estimate the median, quartiles and interquartile range
Draw and interpret box plots
successCriteria: All: draw a cumulative frequency graph with correct plotting points
Most: read the median and quartiles from the graph
Some: draw a box plot and compare two distributions
lessons.crossCurricular: Science and PE: comparing performance data
lessons.smsc: Fair comparison of different groups: use the same measures for both.

keywords.def: a running total of frequencies
upper quartile minus lower quartile
a diagram showing the minimum, quartiles, median and maximum

teach.heading: Cumulative frequency table: test marks of 80 pupils
teach.note: Higher only. Plot each cumulative frequency against the upper class boundary: (10, 4), (20, 14), (30, 36), (40, 62), (50, 76), (60, 80), starting at (0, 0). Join with a smooth curve.

teach.heading: Reading the graph

model.problem: For the 80 marks, estimate the median, lower quartile, upper quartile and interquartile range.
steps: Median at cumulative frequency 40: between 36 (at 30) and 62 (at 40): 30 + 4/26 × 10 ≈ 31.5

teach.note: Read from the graph in an exam: draw lines at 40, 20 and 60 across to the curve and down. Accept a range of values; show the lines. For n values, use n/2, n/4 and 3n/4.

teach.heading: Hinge: quartile position

check.q: In a cumulative frequency graph for 80 values the lower quartile is read at a cumulative frequency of:
check.why: Lower quartile is at 1/4 of the data: 80 ÷ 4 = 20. 40 is the median; 60 the upper quartile.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask for the upper quartile position (60).

teach.heading: Box plot summary
teach.note: Draw the box from the LQ to the UQ with a line at the median and whiskers to the lowest and highest values. Ask what the box represents (middle 50% of the data) and why the IQR ignores outliers.

teach.heading: Comparing

model.problem: Another class has median 36 and IQR 9. Compare with this class (median 31.5, IQR 16.5).
steps: Median: the second class is higher (36 against 31.5) so typically scored more
IQR: the second class is smaller (9 against 16.5) so the marks are more consistent
Conclusion: the second class did better and more consistently
model.answer: Second class higher and more consistent

teach.note: Always give one comment on average and one on spread, with numbers, in context. ANSWERS: practice: 4, 14, 36, 62, 76, 80; median ≈ 31.5, LQ ≈ 22.7, UQ ≈ 39.2, IQR ≈ 16.5; box plot from 3 to 58; second class is higher and more consistent. exit: 60 and 90; the spread of the middle 50% of the data. core: more than 45: 80 - cumulative at 45 (about 69) so about 11; 90th percentile at cumulative frequency 72: 40 + (72 - 62)/14 × 10 ≈ 47.1. extend: IQR = 9; upper fence = 24 + 13.5 = 37.5 so 40 is an outlier. stretch: X has a larger spread (IQR 20 against 11) and a lower middle; Y is more consistent with a higher median. homework: pupil sentences.

practice: Complete the cumulative frequency column for the marks table.
Estimate the median, LQ, UQ and IQR from the graph.
Draw the box plot for the marks.
A second class has median 36 and IQR 9. Compare.
independent: Core: a) Use the graph to estimate how many pupils scored more than 45. b) Estimate the 90th percentile.
Extend: A set of times has min 12, LQ 15, median 18, UQ 24 and max 40. Draw the box plot and find the IQR. State whether 40 is an outlier by the rule UQ + 1.5 × IQR.
Stretch: Compare two box plots: Class X: 20, 35, 42, 55, 80; Class Y: 30, 38, 43, 49, 60 (min, LQ, median, UQ, max).
exit: For 120 values, state the cumulative frequency at which the median and upper quartile are read.
What does the interquartile range measure?
Big question: How can a single graph show the middle and the spread of a large data set?
lessons.homework: Write three comparison sentences for two box plots of your own choice: one about average, one about spread, one about the overall conclusion.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a pre-labelled grid and a table with the plotting points; use rulers for reading. EAL: 'cumulative', 'quartile', 'median'. Stretch: outliers and the 1.5 × IQR rule. Higher-only: cumulative frequency, quartiles, IQR and box plots (S3, S4).
lessons.board: Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9-1) Mathematics (1MA1), Higher tier

lessons.unit: S1-S6: Statistics
lessons.title: Comparing distributions: averages, spread and populations
lessons.bigQuestion: Which average, and which measure of spread, tells the fairest story?
objectives: Estimate the mean from a grouped frequency table
Choose the best average for a situation
Compare distributions using averages and spread and use statistics to describe a population
successCriteria: All: calculate the mean, median and mode from tables
Most: choose a suitable average and measure of spread
Some: compare two distributions in context and combine means
lessons.crossCurricular: Economics and PE: averages in the real world
lessons.smsc: Truthful reporting: the choice of average should not mislead.

keywords.def: the mean found using midpoints of class intervals
a value that is much larger or smaller than the others
how far the data are from the middle

teach.heading: Mean from a grouped table

model.problem: Use the marks table: classes 0-10: 4, 10-20: 10, 20-30: 22, 30-40: 26, 40-50: 14, 50-60: 4. Estimate the mean and give the modal class and median class.
model.answer: Estimated mean 31.0; modal and median class 30-40

teach.note: It is an estimate because we do not know the exact values. Use the midpoint as a representative value.

teach.heading: The best average

model.problem: Five workers earn £22 000, £24 000, £25 000, £26 000 and £150 000. Find the mean and the median, and say which is more representative.
steps: The £150 000 is an outlier pulling the mean up

teach.note: Mean: uses all the values but is affected by extremes. Median: unaffected by outliers. Mode: useful for categorical data or the most common value.

teach.heading: Hinge: the average

check.q: A data set has an extreme outlier. The best average to use is:
check.why: The median is not affected by one extreme value. The range is a measure of spread, not an average.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask which measure of spread is best here (IQR).

teach.heading: Comparing two groups

model.problem: Boys' 100 m times: median 14.2 s, IQR 1.5 s. Girls' times: median 13.8 s, IQR 2.4 s. Compare.
steps: Girls have the lower median so are typically faster
Girls have the higher IQR so are less consistent
Conclusion: girls were faster on average but with more variation
model.answer: Girls faster on average but less consistent

teach.note: Two comments with numbers and context. Use 'typically' and 'on average', not 'all girls'.

teach.heading: Combined mean

model.problem: A class of 20 has mean 62 and a class of 30 has mean 70. Find the mean of all 50.

teach.note: The combined mean is between 62 and 70 and nearer the larger class. It is not (62 + 70) ÷ 2. ANSWERS: practice: 31.0; mean £49 400, median £25 000, so median; girls faster on average but less consistent; 66.8. exit: 5; (10 + 75 + 75) ÷ 10 = 16. core: (a) midpoints 2.5, 7.5, 15: (15 + 105 + 300) ÷ 40 = 10.5; (b) a few high earners raise the mean so it is not typical. extend: the sample mean estimates the population mean, but it varies from sample to sample and depends on random sampling. stretch: the same average but the second set is less consistent. homework: pupil work.

practice: Five workers earn £22 000, £24 000, £25 000, £26 000, £150 000. Find mean and median and choose.
Boys' median 14.2, IQR 1.5; girls' median 13.8, IQR 2.4: compare.
A class of 20 has mean 62 and a class of 30 has mean 70. Find the combined mean.
independent: Core: a) Estimate the mean from: 0-5: 6, 5-10: 14, 10-20: 20. b) A shop reports 'the average wage is £30 000'. Explain how this could mislead.
Extend: A sample of 100 households gives a mean household size of 3.4. Explain how to use this to describe the population, and one limitation.
Stretch: Two data sets have the same mean but different IQRs. Interpret.
exit: Find the mode of 3, 5, 5, 6, 8.
Estimate the mean from a grouped table when the class midpoints are 5, 15, 25 and frequencies 2, 5, 3.
Big question: Which average, and which measure of spread, tells the fairest story?
lessons.homework: Pick two sets of data from the internet (e.g. temperatures of two cities) and compare them using a median and a measure of spread.
lessons.send: SEND: use a table with columns for midpoint and f × midpoint; use a calculator. EAL: 'average', 'spread', 'consistent'. Stretch: weighted means and combined groups. Higher-only: comparing using IQR and combined means; Foundation: mean, median, mode and range.
lessons.board: Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9-1) Mathematics (1MA1), Higher tier

lessons.unit: S1-S6: Statistics
lessons.title: Scatter graphs, correlation and lines of best fit
lessons.bigQuestion: If two things move together, does one cause the other?
objectives: Plot and describe scatter graphs
Draw a line of best fit and use it to estimate
Identify correlation, outliers and the danger of extrapolation
successCriteria: All: describe the type of correlation
Most: draw a line of best fit and make an estimate
Some: explain the difference between correlation and causation and the limits of extrapolation
lessons.crossCurricular: Science and PE: relationships between variables
lessons.smsc: Care in claiming: we do not assert more than the data show.

keywords.def: a relationship between two variables
a straight line drawn through the middle of the points
using the line outside the range of the data

starter: Find the gradient of the line through (1, 35) and (8, 80).
Find y when x = 5.5 in y = 6.2x + 29.

teach.heading: Hours of revision and test score
teach.note: Pupils plot the eight points. They show strong positive correlation. The mean point is (4.5, 57.25). A line of best fit through the mean point has gradient about 6.2 so y ≈ 6.2x + 29.

teach.heading: Using the line

model.problem: Use the line y ≈ 6.2x + 29. Estimate the score for 5.5 hours, and the score for 15 hours. Comment on each.
steps: x = 5.5: y ≈ 6.2 × 5.5 + 29 = 63 (interpolation, within the data range)
122 is impossible if the test has a maximum of 100
Interpolation is reliable; extrapolation may not be

teach.note: The line is a model for the range of the data. Beyond it the relationship may not hold. Accept answers in a range from the pupils' own lines, for example 62 to 65.

teach.heading: Hinge: correlation

check.q: A scatter graph shows strong negative correlation. This means:
options: as x increases, y decreases, with the points close to a line
check.why: Negative: one goes up as the other goes down; strong: points close to the line. A causal claim needs more evidence.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask for an example of negative correlation: the age of a car and its value.

teach.heading: Correlation is not causation

misconception.wrong: Ice cream sales and sunburn cases are correlated, so ice cream causes sunburn.
misconception.right: Both increase because of a third factor: hot sunny weather.

teach.note: Ask for another example. In an exam say 'correlation does not mean causation'; suggest a lurking variable.

teach.heading: Line of best fit rules

model.problem: A car's value (£1000s) against age: (1, 14), (2, 12.5), (3, 11), (5, 8), (6, 7), (8, 4.5). Describe the correlation and estimate the value at 4 years.
steps: Line of best fit: about y = -1.36x + 15.2

teach.note: Drawing rules: pass through the mean point, roughly equal points above and below, ignore outliers. Extrapolate to 12 years gives -1.1: impossible, so extrapolation is unreliable. ANSWERS: practice: strong positive correlation; about 63 (accept 62 to 65); 15 hours is outside the range and gives a score above 100; ice cream sales and sunburn. exit: negative correlation; interpolation is within the range of the data and extrapolation is outside it. core: strong negative; about £9800; at 12 years the line gives about -£1100 which is impossible; the outlier is a special case that should be ignored when drawing the line but mentioned. extend: both depend on age or growth; correlation is not causation. stretch: gradient about -1.36 means the car loses about £1360 in value each year. homework: pupil data.

practice: Plot the eight points of hours against score, describe the correlation and draw a line of best fit.
Use your line to estimate the score for 5.5 hours.
Why is using the line to predict the score for 15 hours unreliable?
Give an example of two variables with correlation but no causation.
independent: Core: a) Plot the car value data and draw a line of best fit. b) Estimate the value at 4 years and comment on the value at 12 years. c) One car is a classic, age 7, value £25 000: what is this point called and what do you do with it?
Extend: A scatter graph of shoe size against height shows positive correlation. Explain whether bigger feet cause greater height.
Stretch: Find the equation of your line of best fit from two points on it, and interpret the gradient in context.
exit: State the type of correlation between age of a car and its value.
Explain the difference between interpolation and extrapolation.
Big question: If two things move together, does one cause the other?
lessons.homework: Collect data from your family or friends (e.g. height and arm span) for 8 people. Plot a scatter graph, describe the correlation and draw a line of best fit.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a pre-drawn grid and a printed table; use a ruler and a clear plotting instruction. EAL: 'correlation', 'outlier', 'extrapolate'. Stretch: use the mean point to build the equation of a line of best fit.
lessons.board: Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9-1) Mathematics (1MA1), Higher tier

lessons.unit: Algebra: Higher graph work and real-life graphs (A13-A16)
lessons.title: Sketching translations and reflections of a given function
lessons.bigQuestion: How does changing a function's equation move its graph?
objectives: Sketch y = f(x) + a, y = f(x + a), y = -f(x) and y = f(-x) from a given graph
Track key points such as maxima, minima and intercepts
Describe the effect of each change on the graph
successCriteria: All: sketch y = f(x) + a and y = -f(x)
Most: sketch y = f(x + a) and y = f(-x)
Some: sketch a combination and identify a transformation from key points
lessons.crossCurricular: Computing: transforming shapes in graphics software
lessons.smsc: Social: seeing the same pattern from different viewpoints

keywords.def: a slide of the graph with no turning or resizing
a mirror image of the graph in an axis
a rule that gives one output for each input
intercepts, turning points and asymptotes to track
a point that does not move

starter: Bismillah. If f(x) = x^2 - 3, find f(2) and f(-2).
What is the turning point of y = (x - 1)^2 + 4?
Write the coordinates of the reflection of (3, 2) in the y-axis.

teach.heading: Four moves, four rules
teach.note: Use f(x) = x(4 - x) with roots (0,0), (4,0) and maximum (2,4). Pupils should know translation by vector from earlier lessons; this lesson is about sketching from a given picture. Rules: f(x) + a moves up by a; f(x + a) moves LEFT by a; -f(x) reflects in the x-axis; f(-x) reflects in the y-axis.

teach.heading: Worked example: translations
teach.note: Draw y = f(x) with max (2,4) and roots 0 and 4. For f(x - 3), every x-coordinate increases by 3: max (5,4), roots (3,0) and (7,0). Emphasise that x-changes happen 'inside the brackets' and do the opposite of what you expect.

model.problem: y = f(x) has a maximum at (2, 4) and crosses the x-axis at (0, 0) and (4, 0). Write the maximum point and the x-intercepts of y = f(x - 3) and of y = f(x) + 1.
steps: f(x - 3): translation by (3, 0), x-values increase by 3
Maximum (2, 4) goes to (5, 4); intercepts (0,0), (4,0) go to (3,0), (7,0)
f(x) + 1: translation by (0, 1), y-values increase by 1
Maximum (2, 4) goes to (2, 5); the roots move off the x-axis because the whole curve is 1 higher

teach.heading: Worked example: reflections
teach.note: Reflection in the x-axis flips y-signs: max (2,4) becomes minimum (2,-4); roots stay at 0 and 4 because they are on the axis. Reflection in the y-axis flips x-signs: max (-2,4), roots (0,0) and (-4,0). Pupils sketch on mini-whiteboards.

model.problem: Using the same f, write the turning point and roots of y = -f(x) and y = f(-x).
steps: Maximum (2, 4) becomes minimum (2, -4); roots stay (0,0) and (4,0)

teach.heading: Common errors
teach.note: The main error is f(x + 2) moves right. Give a memory: x + 2 needs x to be 2 smaller to give the same output, so the graph moves left. Another error: reflecting in the wrong axis. Ask which coordinate has its sign changed.

misconception.wrong: y = f(x + 2) moves the graph 2 to the right
misconception.right: y = f(x + 2) moves the graph 2 to the left (vector (-2, 0))

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer B. A is the wrong direction (right), C is a vertical shift, D is the f(-x) reflection.

check.q: The point (3, 5) is on y = f(x). Which point is on y = f(x + 1)?
check.why: f(x + 1) is a translation by (-1, 0), so (3, 5) goes to (2, 5). (4,5) is the common wrong direction.

practice: A graph y = f(x) has a minimum at (1, -3). Write the minimum of (a) y = f(x) + 4 (b) y = f(x - 2) (c) y = -f(x).
The graph of y = f(x) passes through (-2, 0) and (0, 3). Write one point on y = f(-x).
independent: Core: y = f(x) has a maximum (3, 5) and passes through (0, 0) and (6, 0). Sketch and label y = f(x) + 2 and y = -f(x).
Extend: Using the same graph, sketch y = f(x - 1) and y = f(-x), labelling key points. (4 marks)
Stretch: y = f(x) has a minimum (2, -1). The graph of y = -f(x) + 3 is drawn. Write its turning point and say whether it is a maximum or a minimum. (3 marks)
exit: Write one difference between y = f(x) + 1 and y = f(x + 1).
State the equation of the reflection of y = f(x) in the y-axis.
lessons.homework: On squared paper draw a curve y = f(x) with three labelled points, then draw f(x) + 2 and f(-x) on the same axes.
lessons.send: SEND: tracing paper to slide and flip the curve. EAL: vocabulary matching with 'inside' and 'outside' the brackets. Stretch: sketch y = -f(x - 2) + 1 for a given curve.
lessons.board: Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9-1) Mathematics (1MA1), Higher tier

lessons.unit: Statistics (S1-S6)
lessons.title: Inferring from samples and estimating populations
lessons.bigQuestion: What can a small sample tell us about a large population, and when should we doubt it?
objectives: Use sample data to estimate a population proportion or total
Use capture-recapture to estimate a population size
Describe limitations of sampling and sources of bias
successCriteria: All: scale up a sample proportion
Most: use capture-recapture
Some: evaluate whether a sample result can be trusted
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: ecology and population studies
lessons.smsc: Moral: honesty and care in reporting data

keywords.def: the whole group being studied
a part of the population selected for study
a method for estimating animal population size
unfairness in how a sample is chosen or results are used
a sample that reflects the population

teach.heading: Sample to population
bullets: A sample gives estimates, not exact values.
Estimate a total: population x sample proportion.
Larger, random samples are more reliable.
teach.note: Example: 60 students asked how they travel to school; 21 walk. Proportion 21/60 = 0.35. Estimate for the 1200-student school: 1200 x 0.35 = 420. Emphasise 'estimate' and the assumption that the sample represents everyone.

teach.heading: Worked example: scaling up
teach.note: Check the sampling method: random selection from each year group would be better than only asking Year 7. If the sample was from one class, the estimate may be biased. This links to the lesson on sampling methods.

model.problem: In a random sample of 60 students, 21 walk to school. The school has 1200 students. Estimate how many walk.

teach.heading: Capture-recapture
teach.note: Story: 40 fish are caught, tagged and returned to the lake. After mixing, 50 fish are caught and 8 are tagged. Assume the sample proportion tagged (8/50) equals the population proportion tagged (40/N). So N = 40 x 50 / 8 = 250. State the assumptions: no births, deaths or migration in between, tagged fish mix evenly, tags do not harm survival or make fish easier to catch.

model.problem: 40 fish are tagged and released. Later, 50 fish are caught, of which 8 are tagged. Estimate the number of fish in the lake.

teach.heading: Limitations
bullets: Small or biased samples can mislead.
teach.note: Ask pupils: if the second catch were from the same corner of the lake, what happens? Discuss non-response, small samples and a sampling frame that leaves out part of the population. Link to Islamic ethics: presenting data honestly and not claiming more than the evidence supports.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer B. A sample of 20 is small, and the sample is only from one year group; both are limitations. Option C is an error: the sample proportion is not the population number.

check.q: A survey of 15 pupils from one Year 7 class finds 9 prefer football. A student says 60% of the whole school prefers football. What is the main problem?
options: The sample is small and unrepresentative
check.why: 9/15 = 60% is correct, but 15 pupils from one class may not represent the school.

practice: In a random sample of 80 adults, 28 own a bicycle. Estimate how many of 5000 adults own a bicycle.
50 deer are tagged. A later sample of 40 contains 5 tagged deer. Estimate the deer population.
independent: Core: In a sample of 25 batteries, 3 are faulty. Estimate the number of faulty batteries in a batch of 2000.
Extend: 30 birds are ringed. A later sample of 60 birds includes 9 ringed. Estimate the population and state one assumption. (4 marks)
Stretch: Explain two reasons why a capture-recapture estimate might be too high or too low. (4 marks)
exit: Write the formula you used for capture-recapture in words.
Why is a larger random sample better than a small one?
lessons.homework: Find a real example of a statistic in the news based on a sample. Say what the population is and one possible limitation.
lessons.send: SEND: step cards with 'tagged / sample / total'. EAL: pictures of the lake. Stretch: explain why the formula rearranges to N = (M x n)/m.

lessons.unit: Statistics (S1-S6)
lessons.title: Histograms with unequal class widths: frequency density
lessons.bigQuestion: Why must the height of a bar be frequency density, not frequency?
objectives: Calculate frequency density = frequency / class width
Draw and read histograms with unequal class widths
Estimate frequencies from parts of a bar
successCriteria: All: calculate frequency density
Most: complete a histogram and read frequencies
Some: estimate counts within bars and find missing information
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: population age data
lessons.smsc: Social: representing data fairly (not misleading)

keywords.def: frequency divided by class width
the size of the interval
a chart where area represents frequency
data measured on a scale, such as time or height
an approximate value found assuming even spread within a class

starter: Class 10 < t <= 30: what is its width?
What is the difference between a bar chart and a histogram?

teach.heading: Why frequency density?
bullets: Classes with different widths cannot be compared by height alone.
In a histogram, area of bar = frequency.
teach.note: Show an example where a wide class has the highest frequency but the bars would mislead if drawn by frequency. Explain that area is what represents frequency. The vertical axis is labelled frequency density. Bars touch because the data is continuous.

teach.heading: Worked example: drawing
teach.note: Table: time t minutes: 0<t<=10 frequency 15; 10<t<=30 frequency 50; 30<t<=40 frequency 30; 40<t<=60 frequency 20. Widths 10, 20, 10, 20. FD: 1.5, 2.5, 3, 1. Check frequency = FD x width: 1.5 x 10 = 15. Pupils sketch the four bars.

model.problem: Find the frequency densities for: 0<t<=10 (15), 10<t<=30 (50), 30<t<=40 (30), 40<t<=60 (20).

teach.heading: Worked example: reading and estimating
teach.note: A bar from 20 to 50 has height 0.8: width 30, frequency 24. To estimate the number between 20 and 30 in the 10 to 30 class (FD 2.5): the section from 20 to 30 is 10 wide, so 10 x 2.5 = 25. This assumes the data is evenly spread across the class; say so. From 30 to 40: 30. So between 20 and 40: 25 + 30 = 55.

model.problem: Using the table above, estimate how many times were between 20 and 40 minutes.
steps: The class 10-30 has FD 2.5, so 20-30 is 10 x 2.5 = 25

teach.heading: Common errors
teach.note: Plotting frequency as bar height is the standard mistake. Another is calculating a bar's frequency as height only. Give: frequency = FD x class width, always.

misconception.wrong: The height of a bar is its frequency
misconception.right: The area of a bar is its frequency; height is frequency density

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer C: 4 x 5 = 20. A is the height, B the width, D adds them.

check.q: A histogram bar covers 10 < x <= 15 and has frequency density 4. What is the frequency?
check.why: Frequency = frequency density x class width = 4 x 5 = 20.

practice: Complete: class 0<x<=5, frequency 20; 5<x<=15, frequency 45; 15<x<=35, frequency 30. Work out the frequency densities.
A bar has width 8 and height 2.5. Find its frequency.
independent: Extend: In a histogram, bar 10<x<=20 has frequency density 1.2 and bar 20<x<=40 has frequency 18. Find the density of the second and the number in the first. (3 marks)
Stretch: Estimate the number of values greater than 15 in a class 10<x<=20 with frequency 40, and the next class 20<x<=30 with frequency 25. (3 marks)
exit: Write the formula for frequency density.
Why do we use frequency density instead of frequency on the vertical axis?
lessons.homework: Find or invent a grouped table with unequal classes. Work out the frequency densities and sketch the histogram.
lessons.send: SEND: pre-drawn axes and a calculator. EAL: key words glossary with diagram. Stretch: estimate the median from a histogram.

lessons.unit: Statistics (S1-S6)
lessons.title: Cumulative frequency graphs: median, quartiles and estimates
lessons.bigQuestion: What can a cumulative frequency curve tell us at a glance?
objectives: Build a cumulative frequency table and plot the graph
Estimate the median, quartiles and interquartile range
Estimate how many values lie above or below a given value
successCriteria: All: calculate cumulative frequencies
Most: plot and read the median
Some: find IQR and estimate numbers above a value
lessons.crossCurricular: Business: delivery times and quality control
lessons.smsc: Moral: reading evidence carefully before judging

keywords.def: a running total of frequencies
the middle value, at n/2
values at n/4 and 3n/4
upper quartile minus lower quartile
the largest value in a class, where its point is plotted

starter: What is the IQR if Q1 = 20 and Q3 = 36?

teach.heading: Cumulative frequency
bullets: Plot against the UPPER class boundary.
teach.note: Table: parcel mass m (kg): 0<m<=10: 4; 10<m<=20: 12; 20<m<=30: 24; 30<m<=40: 28; 40<m<=50: 12; total 80. Cumulative frequency 4, 16, 40, 68, 80, plotted at m = 10, 20, 30, 40, 50. Plot (0,0) as an extra start point if asked. Common error: plotting at the middle of the class.

teach.heading: Reading the curve
bullets: Lower quartile at n/4; upper quartile at 3n/4.
teach.note: With n = 80: median at the 40th value, LQ at the 20th, UQ at the 60th. Read across then down. From the data the curve passes through (30,40) so the median is 30 kg. Pupils should show construction lines on the graph.

model.problem: For the 80 parcels, estimate the lower quartile and upper quartile using straight lines between points. Then find the IQR.
steps: LQ is the 20th value, between (20, 16) and (30, 40): 20 + (4/24) x 10 = 21.7
UQ is the 60th value, between (30, 40) and (40, 68): 30 + (20/28) x 10 = 37.1
model.answer: LQ about 21.7 kg, UQ about 37.1 kg, IQR about 15.4 kg

teach.heading: Estimating numbers above a value
teach.note: Estimate the number above 35 kg. At 35, between (30,40) and (40,68): 40 + 0.5 x 28 = 54. So 80 - 54 = 26 parcels exceed 35 kg. On a drawn smooth curve readings may differ slightly; accept answers close to 26.

model.problem: Estimate how many parcels weigh more than 35 kg.
steps: Cumulative frequency at 35 kg is halfway between 40 and 68

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer B. A plots at the middle of the class. C confuses the median with the position. D uses the lower boundary.

check.q: Where should the cumulative frequency for the class 20 < m <= 30 be plotted?
check.why: Cumulative frequency counts values up to the upper class boundary, so the point is plotted at m = 30.

practice: Complete the cumulative frequency table: 0<x<=10: 3; 10<x<=20: 9; 20<x<=30: 18; 30<x<=40: 12.
For a graph with 60 values, at which cumulative frequencies do you read the median and quartiles?
independent: Core: Use the data above to plot the parcel graph and read the median.
Extend: A second depot has median 28 kg and IQR 10 kg. Compare it with the first depot (median 30, IQR 15.4). (2 marks)
Stretch: Estimate the number of parcels between 15 kg and 35 kg. (3 marks)
exit: How do you find the LQ from a graph with 120 values?
Why do you plot at the upper boundary?
lessons.homework: Collect 20 values of a measurement from home (for example, heights of family members' shoes), group them and draw a cumulative frequency graph.
lessons.send: SEND: plot points on pre-drawn axes. EAL: labelled graph with median, LQ and UQ. Stretch: draw a box plot from the same graph.

lessons.title: Revision: fractions, recurring decimals and surds
lessons.bigQuestion: Which number skills must be secure without leaning on a calculator?
objectives: To understand how to calculate exactly with fractions, recurring decimals and surds in exam questions
successCriteria: All: calculate with mixed numbers and convert a recurring decimal to a fraction
Most: simplify, expand and rationalise surds
Some: answer 'show that' surd questions with every step shown
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: the same algebra and number skills are used in International GCSE Physics and Chemistry calculations
lessons.smsc: Moral: preparing thoroughly for exams is part of ihsan (إِحْسَان), doing a task as well as possible

keywords.def: an exact root such as √5
remove a surd from the denominator
a decimal that repeats for ever
give every step to reach the stated answer

hook.text: Your calculator gives 1.732050808 for √3. Why might an examiner prefer the answer √3, and when would a decimal be fine?
hook.a: √3 is exact; any decimal is rounded. Questions saying 'exact' or 'show that' need surds; 'give your answer to 3 s.f.' wants a decimal.

teach.heading: Mixed numbers and recurring decimals
bullets: Recurring: multiply to match the repeating tails
teach.note: Show both models briefly; pupils then do the practice.

model.problem: Write 0.3666... as a fraction in its simplest form.

teach.heading: Surds
teach.note: Rationalise a ± √b denominators with the conjugate.

model.problem: Rationalise 5/(√7 − 2).

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Teams poll: launch it, give 30 seconds, then share the results.

check.why: 5 − 1 = 4. 6 adds instead of subtracting.

teach.heading: Exam technique
bullets: 'Show that': every step, no calculator jumps
Give exact answers unless told to round
teach.note: Mark scheme: M1 for a correct method, A1 for the stated answer reached with working.

head: Command
What earns the marks
rows: Every step written; final line equals the given answer
Give your answer in its simplest form
Fractions, surds or π, not rounded decimals

practice.q: Show that 1 3/5 × 2 1/12 = 3 1/3. (3 marks)
Write 0.2151515... as a fraction in its simplest form. (3 marks)
Expand and simplify (5 − √3)².
Rationalise 14/√7.

independent.q: Extend (2 marks): Show that (√18 + √2)/√2 = 4.
Stretch (3 marks): Rationalise and simplify (3 + √5)/(3 − √5).

exit.q: Write 0.444... as a fraction.
Work out √27 × √3.

lessons.title: Revision: indices and standard form
lessons.bigQuestion: How do the index laws unlock both algebra and standard form?
objectives: To understand how to use the index laws with numbers, algebra and standard form in exam questions
successCriteria: All: evaluate negative and fractional indices
Most: simplify algebraic powers and calculate in standard form
Some: solve equations by writing both sides with the same base
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: the mass of atoms and the Avogadro constant are written in standard form
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: from atoms to galaxies, standard form lets us describe the scale of creation

keywords.def: a power
A × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ A < 10
1 ÷ the number
the number being raised to a power

hook.text: A hydrogen atom has a mass of about 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. How could you estimate how many atoms are in 1 kg of hydrogen?

teach.heading: Index laws with algebra
bullets: Powers of letters follow the same laws
Apply the power to every factor in the bracket

model.problem: Simplify (8x⁶)^(2/3).

teach.heading: Standard form without a calculator
bullets: Divide the numbers, subtract the powers
teach.note: Paper 1H and 2H both allow calculators, but setting work out shows the method.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Teams poll: launch it, give 30 seconds, then share the results.

check.why: 15 × 10⁻³ = 1.5 × 10⁻². 15 × 10⁻³ is equal but not in standard form.

teach.heading: Same base equations
bullets: Write both sides as powers of the same number

misconception.right: The 2 is raised to the power too: 16x¹²

practice.q: Evaluate (16/81)^(−3/4). (2 marks)
practice.model: Negative index: flip the fraction: (81/16)^(3/4). Fourth root: 3/2. Cube: 27/8.

practice.q: Simplify (5x²y³)² ÷ xy.
Work out (2.4 × 10⁶) ÷ (8 × 10⁻³) in standard form.
Solve 3^(2x) = 81.

independent.q: Core: (a) Evaluate 125^(−2/3) (b) Simplify (3a⁴b)³ (c) Work out (4.2 × 10⁵) + (3 × 10⁴) in standard form (d) Simplify √(9x⁸)
Extend (2 marks): The mass of a hydrogen atom is 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. How many hydrogen atoms are in 1 kg? Give your answer in standard form to 3 s.f.
Stretch (4 marks): 2ᵃ × 4ᵇ = 64 and 3ᵃ ÷ 9ᵇ = 1. Find a and b.
independent.a: a + 2b = 6 and a − 2b = 0, so a = 3, b = 1.5

exit.q: Evaluate 64^(−1/2).
Work out (2 × 10³)².

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Revision cycle 1: Number, algebra, sequences, graphs
lessons.title: Revision: upper and lower bounds
lessons.bigQuestion: How wrong could an answer be when the measurements are rounded?
objectives: To understand how to find and use upper and lower bounds in calculations
successCriteria: All: write the bounds of a rounded measurement
Most: find the maximum or minimum of a sum, difference, product or quotient
Some: give an answer to a suitable degree of accuracy using the bounds
lessons.crossCurricular: Physics: every measurement has an uncertainty, which limits the accuracy of calculated results
lessons.smsc: Moral: honest reporting of how accurate a result really is

keywords.def: the largest value that rounds to the measurement
the smallest value that rounds to the measurement
LB ≤ x < UB
how precisely a value is given

hook.text: A car travels 245 km (to the nearest 5 km) in 3.5 hours (to the nearest 0.1 hour). How fast could it have gone at most? How sure can we be of its speed?
hook.a: Max speed = 247.5 ÷ 3.45 ≈ 71.7 km/h; min = 242.5 ÷ 3.55 ≈ 68.3 km/h. Both round to 70 km/h to 1 s.f.

starter.q: Write the error interval for 6 rounded to the nearest whole number.

teach.heading: Which bounds give the maximum?
bullets: Subtract and divide: upper with lower
teach.note: 4MA1 1.8A (Higher).

teach.heading: Model
bullets: Write the bounds first, then calculate
teach.note: Area of a 7.4 cm by 3.2 cm rectangle (both to 1 d.p.).

model.problem: Find the bounds of the area of a 7.4 cm by 3.2 cm rectangle (1 d.p.).

teach.heading: Common error
bullets: Divide by the lower bound for a maximum
teach.note: Ask: does dividing by a smaller number give more or less?

misconception.wrong: Max speed = UB distance ÷ UB time
misconception.right: Max speed = UB distance ÷ LB time

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Teams poll: launch it, give 30 seconds, then share the results.

check.q: x = 4.6 to 1 decimal place. What is the upper bound?
check.why: Half of 0.1 above: 4.65. 4.69 is not the bound; 4.7 rounds to 4.7.

practice.q: Write the bounds of 250 g to the nearest 10 g.
practice.model: Nearest 10 g: half of 10 is 5. Lower bound 250 − 5 = 245 g; upper bound 250 + 5 = 255 g.

practice.q: Find the lower bound of 12.6 + 4.3 (each 1 d.p.).
Find the maximum of 8.4 − 2.7 (each 1 d.p.).
Find the upper bound of 24 ÷ 1.5 (24 to the nearest whole, 1.5 to 1 d.p.).

independent.q: Core: A square has side 8.6 cm to 1 d.p. Find the bounds of its perimeter and its area.
independent.a: Perimeter 34.2 to 34.6 cm; area 73.1025 to 74.8225 cm²

independent.q: Extend (3 marks): d = 245 km to the nearest 5 km and t = 3.5 h to the nearest 0.1 h. Find the upper bound of the average speed.
Stretch (2 marks): Find the lower bound of the speed and use both bounds to give the speed to a suitable degree of accuracy.
independent.a: 242.5 ÷ 3.55 = 68.3; both bounds round to 70 km/h to 1 s.f., so 70 km/h

exit.q: Write the lower bound of 3.7 m to 1 d.p.
Which bounds give the maximum of a − b?
exit.a: Upper bound of a minus lower bound of b

lessons.title: Revision: percentages, growth and ratio
lessons.bigQuestion: Which multiplier solves which percentage question?
objectives: To understand how to choose and use multipliers and ratio methods in exam questions

Most: solve repeated change and ratio problems
Some: find a rate from repeated change and combine ratios

keywords.def: the decimal for a percentage change
finding the original
fall in value over time
a comparison of parts

hook.text: A price goes up 20% and then down 20%. Has it returned to the start? What single multiplier describes both changes?
hook.a: No: 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96, a 4% fall overall.

starter.q: Write the multiplier for a 4% decrease.
After 15% off, a price is £76.50. Find the original.
y is proportional to x and y = 12 when x = 3. Write y in terms of x.

teach.heading: Choosing the method
teach.note: Pupils sort question types on whiteboards.

teach.heading: Islamic note: riba
bullets: Islamic finance uses partnership and cost-plus sale
teach.note: Islamic note: riba (رِبَا) is forbidden (Qur'an 2:275: Allah has permitted trade and forbidden riba). Islamic finance uses partnership (mushārakah, مُشَارَكَة) and cost-plus sale (murābaḥah, مُرَابَحَة) instead. Compound interest is examined (1.6), so we answer it accurately as knowledge, never as something to take.

quote.text: Allah has permitted trade and forbidden riba.

teach.heading: Ratio model
bullets: Make the shared part the same

model.problem: A : B = 2 : 3 and B : C = 4 : 5. A + B + C = 175. Find C.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Teams poll: launch it, give 30 seconds, then share the results.

check.q: £800 depreciates by 10% a year. What is it worth after 2 years?

Share £540 in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4.
A population of 8,000 falls by 2.5% a year. Find it after 3 years, to the nearest whole number.
a : b = 3 : 7 and b − a = 28. Find a + b.

independent.q: Core: (a) Increase £360 by 17.5% (b) Write 48 as a percentage of 320 (c) A van worth £12,000 depreciates by 15% a year. Find its value after 3 years.
Extend (3 marks): In the wider economy, an amount grows by r% compound interest each year, from £5,000 to £5,624.32 in 3 years. Find r.

Share 63 in the ratio 4 : 5.

lessons.title: Revision: linear equations and rearranging formulae
lessons.bigQuestion: How do we keep an equation balanced however complicated it looks?

keywords.def: an equation where the unknown has power 1
the letter on its own
take out a common factor
lowest common multiple

hook.text: In the formula y = (x + 2)/x, x appears twice. How can we ever get x on its own?

teach.note: Pupils then do a practice question.

keywords.def: rate of change: speed or acceleration
on a speed-time graph, the distance travelled
rate of change of speed (m/s²)
slowing down

hook.text: A car's speed-time graph has a sloping line, a flat line and another slope. What story does it tell, and how far did the car go?
hook.a: Speeding up, steady speed, slowing down. The distance is the area under the graph.

starter.q: Find the average speed for 150 km in 2.5 h.
Area of a trapezium with parallel sides 4 and 10, height 6?

teach.heading: Two kinds of graph
teach.note: 4MA1 3.3A, and 3.4E later with calculus.

teach.heading: Model
bullets: Split the area into triangles and rectangles
teach.note: 0 to 20 m/s in 8 s, 20 m/s for 12 s, then to 0 in 5 s.

model.problem: Find the acceleration and the total distance.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Teams poll: launch it, give 30 seconds, then share the results.

check.q: The area under a speed-time graph gives the...
check.why: Speed × time = distance. The gradient gives acceleration.

teach.heading: Common error
bullets: Distance is the area, not the height
teach.note: Ask: what are the units of the area?

misconception.wrong: Distance = the highest speed on the graph
misconception.right: Distance = area under the speed-time graph

practice.q: A train accelerates from 4 m/s to 16 m/s in 6 s. Find the acceleration and the distance. (3 marks)
practice.model: Acceleration = change in speed ÷ time = 12 ÷ 6 = 2 m/s². Distance = area of trapezium = ½ × (4 + 16) × 6 = 60 m.

practice.q: Find the average speed for 40 km in 50 minutes, in km/h.
A car slows from 20 m/s to rest in 5 s. Find the deceleration.
Distance travelled in 10 s at a constant 15 m/s?

Stretch: A distance-time graph is curved. Explain how to estimate the speed at one moment.
independent.a: Draw a tangent at that point and find its gradient

exit.q: A speed-time triangle has base 6 s and height 18 m/s. Distance?
What is its acceleration?

the value of k

misconception.right: y = k/x: the product xy stays constant

the gradient at a point
a line joining two points on a curve

hook.text: You have an accurate graph of y = x² − 2x − 3. Could it help you solve x² − 4x − 1 = 0 without the formula? How?
hook.a: Yes: rearrange to x² − 2x − 3 = 2x − 2, draw y = 2x − 2 and read where it crosses the curve.

starter.q: Rearrange x² − 3x = 1 so it equals zero.
What is a tangent to a curve?
starter.a: A line touching the curve at one point

teach.heading: The curve
bullets: Solutions of x² − 2x − 3 = k: draw y = k

teach.heading: Which line to draw?
bullets: Make one side the drawn curve
The other side is the line
teach.note: x² − 4x − 1 = 0 becomes x² − 2x − 3 = 2x − 2.

model.problem: Which line solves x² − 3x − 5 = 0 using the graph of y = x² − 2x − 3?

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Teams poll: launch it, give 30 seconds, then share the results.

check.q: To solve x² − 2x − 3 = 2 from the graph of y = x² − 2x − 3, which line do you draw?
check.why: Read where the curve has height 2.

teach.heading: Gradient of a curve
bullets: Draw a tangent and find its gradient
Or use a short chord either side
teach.note: y = x² at x = 3: chord from 2.9 to 3.1 gives (9.61 − 8.41) ÷ 0.2 = 6.

misconception.wrong: The gradient of y = x² at x = 3 is 9 (the y value)
misconception.right: It is the gradient of the tangent at (3, 9), which is 6

practice.q: Find where y = 2x meets y = x² − 3. (3 marks)
practice.model: Set equal: x² − 3 = 2x, so x² − 2x − 3 = 0, (x − 3)(x + 1) = 0, x = 3 or −1. y = 2x gives (3, 6) and (−1, −2).

practice.q: Solve x² − 2x − 3 = 5.

independent.a: (9.61 − 8.41) ÷ 0.2 = 6; the chord is very short and centred on x = 3, so it is close to the tangent

practice.q: OA = a, OB = b, M is the midpoint of AB. Find OM.
practice.model: OM = OA + ½AB = a + ½(b - a) = ½a + ½b.

AB = 3a + b and BC = 6a + 2b. What can you say about A, B and C?

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 12 marks): OABC is a parallelogram with OA = a and OC = c. M is the midpoint of AB and N is on CB with CN : NB = 2 : 1. (a) Find AB, OM and ON in terms of a and c [4] (b) Find MN [2] (c) X is on OB with OX : XB = 3 : 1. Find OX [2] (d) P is the point with OP = 2a + c. Prove that O, M and P are collinear [4]
independent.a: (a) AB = c, OM = a + ½c, ON = c + ⅔a (b) MN = ½c - ⅓a (c) OB = a + c, OX = ¾(a + c) (d) OP = 2(a + ½c) = 2 OM, sharing O, so O, M, P are collinear
independent.model:
(a) AB = OC = c; OM = a + ½c; ON = c + ⅔a (CB = a).
(b) ON - OM = ⅔a + c - a - ½c = ½c - ⅓a.
(c) ¾ of OB.
(d) as shown.

independent.q: Extend (4 marks): In triangle OAB, OA = a, OB = b. P divides OA in the ratio 1 : 2 and Q divides OB in the ratio 1 : 2. Prove PQ is parallel to AB and find the ratio PQ : AB.
independent.a: PQ = ⅓b - ⅓a = ⅓(b - a) = ⅓AB; parallel, ratio 1 : 3

exit.q: To prove collinear you need a multiple AND
Big question: how do vectors prove lines are parallel?
exit.a: If one vector is a scalar multiple of the other, the lines are parallel.

model.problem: A right-angled triangle has adjacent side 5 cm and opposite side 7 cm. Find the angle, then the hypotenuse.
steps: Use the stored value: hypotenuse = 5 ÷ cos 54.462...° = 8.60
Rounding θ to 54° first gives 8.51: wrong

teach.heading: Pacing and checking
bullets: Stuck: write a method, mark it, move on
Last 10 minutes: return, then check units and rounding
teach.note: The 'checking' minutes are worth marks.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Teams poll: launch it, give 30 seconds, then share the results.

check.q: 'Give your answer in terms of π' for the area of a circle of radius 5 cm. You write:
check.why: Leave π in: 25π cm². The decimals are correct values but not in the form asked.

practice.q: Show that the area of an equilateral triangle of side 6 cm is 9√3 cm².
practice.model:
Area = ½ × 6 × 6 × sin 60° = 18 × √3/2.
= 9√3 cm²: every step written because the answer is given.

independent.q: Timed mixed section (portal, 20 minutes, 22 marks; command words highlighted). Sample: (a) show that the solutions of x² - 4x - 3 = 0 are 2 ± √7 [3] (b) the volume of a cone of radius 3 cm and height 8 cm, in terms of π [2] (c) a rectangle is 8.4 cm by 5.2 cm, each to 1 d.p.: the upper bound of its perimeter [2] (d) the exact value of (√12 + √3)² [3]
independent.model:
(a) Complete the square: (x - 2)² - 4 - 3 = 0 (M1); (x - 2)² = 7 (M1); x = 2 ± √7 (A1). Every step shown, because the answer is given.
(d) √12 = 2√3, so (3√3)² = 27.

independent.q: Extend: explain in the portal response box why 'x = 2.6' alone earns no marks when the question says 'show that the root is 2.6 to 1 d.p.'.
independent.a: The answer is given, so the marks are for the method and for a more accurate value (such as 2.63) that rounds to 2.6.

exit.q: Is the cosine rule on the 4MA1 Higher formulae sheet?
Which must you learn: the area of a circle or the volume of a sphere?
Big question: how can you gain marks on questions you cannot finish?
exit.a: Write a method for every part, use exact or unrounded values, follow the command words and return to unfinished parts at the end.

teach.note: Tree diagram.

model.problem: A box has 7 green and 5 yellow beads. Two are taken without replacement. Find P(both the same colour).

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Teams poll: launch it, give 30 seconds, then share the results.

check.q: For the upper bound of p - q, use:
options: upper bound of p minus lower bound of q
lower bound of p minus upper bound of q
check.why: To make a difference as big as possible, take the biggest p and the smallest q.

practice.q: The upper bound of p - q when p = 24.6 and q = 3.2 (both 1 d.p.).
